==Problem==

When three positive integers <imath>a</imath>, <imath>b</imath>, and <imath>c</imath> are multiplied together, their product is <imath>100</imath>. Suppose <imath>a < b < c</imath>. In how many ways can the numbers be chosen?

<imath>\textbf{(A) } 0 \qquad \textbf{(B) } 1\qquad\textbf{(C) } 2\qquad\textbf{(D) } 3\qquad\textbf{(E) } 4</imath>

==Solution 1==

The positive divisors of <imath>100</imath> are <cmath>1,2,4,5,10,20,25,50,100.</cmath>
It is clear that <imath>10\leq c\leq50,</imath> so we apply casework to <imath>c:</imath>

* If <imath>c=10,</imath> then <imath>(a,b,c)=(2,5,10).</imath>

* If <imath>c=20,</imath> then <imath>(a,b,c)=(1,5,20).</imath>

* If <imath>c=25,</imath> then <imath>(a,b,c)=(1,4,25).</imath>

* If <imath>c=50,</imath> then <imath>(a,b,c)=(1,2,50).</imath>

Together, the numbers <imath>a,b,</imath> and <imath>c</imath> can be chosen in <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(E) } 4}</imath> ways.

~MRENTHUSIASM

==Solution 2==

The positive divisors of <imath>100</imath> are <cmath>1,2,4,5,10,20,25,50,100.</cmath>
We apply casework to <imath>a</imath>:

If <imath>a=1</imath>, then there are <imath>3</imath> cases:

* <imath>b=2,c=50</imath>

* <imath>b=4,c=25</imath>

* <imath>b=5,c=20</imath>

If <imath>a=2</imath>, then there is only <imath>1</imath> case:

* <imath>b=5,c=10</imath>

In total, there are <imath>3+1=\boxed{\textbf{(E) } 4}</imath> ways to choose distinct positive integer values of <imath>a,b,c</imath>.

~MathFun1000
